query: Can the Supreme Court exercise powers under Article 142 of the Constitution to grant admission to an IIT candidate from a marginalized community who was prevented from paying fees due to a portal login glitch?
rationale: Direct positive holding in Atul Kumar v. Chairman JOSAA that power under Article 142 to do substantial justice covers a talented student from a marginalized group left in the lurch by online portal login glitches.

passages.case_title: ATUL KUMAR versus THE CHAIRMAN (JOINT SEAT ALLOCATION AUTHORITY) AND OTHERS
passages.passage_text:
Held: Petitioner logged in as many as on six occasions and 
uploaded the documents, which evidently indicates that he was 
making earnest efforts to log into the portal – No conceivable 
reason why the petitioner would not have done so if he had the 
wherewithal to pay the fees of Rs 17,500 – Talented student like 
the petitioner who belongs to a marginalized group of citizens 
and has done everything to secure admission should not be left 
in the lurch – Power of this Court u/Art.142 to do substantial 
justice is meant precisely to cover such a situation – Petitioner 
to be granted admission to IIT Dhanbad against the seat which 
was allotted to him in the branch of Electrical Engineering  – 
Supernumerary seat to be created for the petitioner, if so 
required. [Paras 6, 7]

query: Can any person aggrieved by an order of the NCLAT maintain an appeal before the Supreme Court under Section 62 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code?
rationale: Direct positive holding in Glas Trust v. Byju Raveendran that Section 62 IBC uses 'any person aggrieved' indicating no rigid locus requirement, so any stakeholder creditor can maintain an appeal.

passages.case_title: GLAS TRUST COMPANY LLC  versus BYJU RAVEENDRAN & ORS.
passages.passage_text:

the Supreme Court from the orders of the NCLAT, “any person” 
aggrieved by the order of the NCLAT may file an appeal before 
the Supreme Court – Section 61 which provides for appeals to 
NCLAT from orders of the NCLT uses similar language – The 
use of the phrase “any person aggrieved” indicates that there is 
no rigid locus requirement to institute an appeal challenging an 
order of the NCLT, before the NCLAT or an order of the NCLAT, 
before this Court – Any person who is aggrieved by the order may

query: Does an FIR under Section 420 IPC require dishonest inducement with mens rea since inception to survive quashing under Section 482 CrPC?
rationale: Direct positive holding in HDFC Bank v. State of Bihar that Section 420 IPC requires inducement since inception, fraudulent inducement, and mens rea; in their absence FIR is liable to be quashed.

passages.case_title: HDFC BANK LTD. versus THE STATE OF BIHAR & ORS.
passages.passage_text:
Held: The FIR must disclose the following ingredients to make out 
an offence u/s.420 : (i) That the Accused has induced anyone since 
inception; (ii) That the inducement was fraudulent or dishonest; 
(iii) That mens rea existed at the time of such inducement. The 
Accused/Bank is a jurisdiction person, and as such, the question of 
mens rea does not arise. However, on reading of the F.I.R., there 
is nothing to show that the Accused/Bank or its staff members had 
dishonestly induced someone to deceived to deliver any property 
to any person, and that the mens rea existed at the time of such 
inducement – Thus, the ingredients to attract the offence u/s.420 
I.P.C. would not be available. [Paras 20 and 21]

query: Does the Hindu legal concept of joint family coparcenary property apply to Mohammedans governed by Muslim law?
rationale: Direct negative holding in Nisar Ahmad v. Sami Ullah that the concept of joint family property prevalent amongst Hindus is not known amongst Muslims and cannot be imported.

passages.case_title: NISAR AHMAD & ORS. versus SAMI ULLAH (DEAD) THROUGH LRS. & ANR.
passages.passage_text:
Held: No error or perversity in the view taken by the High Court – 
The concept of joint family property which is prevalent amongst the 
Hindus is not known amongst the Muslims

query: Does an error of judgment or difference of medical opinion between doctors ipso facto establish criminal or civil negligence?
rationale: Direct negative holding in Neeraj Sud v. Jaswinder Singh that an error of judgment or accident is not sufficient proof of negligence so long as the doctor followed acceptable medical practice.

passages.case_title: NEERAJ SUD AND ANR.  versus JASWINDER SINGH (MINOR) AND ANR.
passages.passage_text:
However, a simple lack of care, an error of judgment 
or an accident is not sufficient proof of negligence on part of the 
medical professional so long as the doctor follows the acceptable 
practice of the medical profession in discharge of his duties – He 
cannot be held liable for negligence merely because a better 
alternative treatment or course of treatment was available or that 
more skilled doctors were there who could have administered 
better treatment. [Para 14]

query: Does Section 36A(5) of the NDPS Act empower a Special Judge to conduct summary trial for offences punishable with imprisonment exceeding three years?
rationale: Bharti Arora v. State of Haryana holds that Section 36A(5) NDPS Act permits summary trials only for offences punishable with imprisonment of not more than three years, and such proceedings can only be conducted by a Magistrate.

passages.case_title: BHARTI ARORA versus THE STATE OF HARYANA
passages.passage_text:
s.36-A (5) of the NDPS Act which begins with the non-obstante 
clause provides that notwithstanding anything contained in the 
Cr.P.C., the offences punishable under this Act with imprisonment 
for a term of not more than three years may be tried summarily – 
So, the statutory scheme, according to the provisions of s.36-A(5) 
of the NDPS Act, prescribes that, for convicting a person u/s. 
58 of the NDPS Act, he/she must be tried summarily – Further, 
s.260 of the Cr.P.C. provides that the power to try summarily is 
with any Judicial Magistrate, any Metropolitan Magistrate or any 
Magistrate of the first class specially empowered in this behalf by 
the High Court – It is thus clear that the Special Judge could not 
have conducted the proceedings against the present appellant for 
the offence punishable u/s.58 of the NDPS Act inasmuch as such 
proceedings could have been conducted only by a Magistrate

query: Does Section 65 of the PMLA exempt the prosecution from obtaining prior sanction under Section 197 of the CrPC when prosecuting a public servant?
rationale: Bibhu Prasad Acharya holds that Section 65 PMLA makes CrPC applicable and is not inconsistent with Section 197(1) CrPC; prior sanction is mandatory and not exempted.

passages.case_title: DIRECTORATE OF ENFORCEMENT versus BIBHU PRASAD ACHARYA, ETC.
passages.passage_text:
As far as the applicability of s.197 of CrPC to the 
PMLA is concerned, there are two relevant provisions in the form 
of s.65 and 71 of the PMLA – S.65 makes the provisions of the 
CrPC applicable to all proceedings under the PMLA, provided 
the same are not inconsistent with the provisions contained in 
the PMLA – The words ‘All other proceedings’ in s.65 include a 
complaint u/s.44 (1)(b) of the PMLA – There is no provision therein 
which is inconsistent with the provisions of s.197(1) of CrPC – 
Therefore, the provisions of s.197(1) of CrPC are applicable to a 
complaint u/s.44(1)(b) of the PMLA

query: Can criminal proceedings under Section 498A IPC be sustained on general and vague allegations intended only to exert pressure in a civil property dispute?
rationale: Kailashben Patel v. State of Maharashtra holds that criminal proceedings instituted with mala fide intention on general, vague, and omnibus allegations to further civil property disputes cannot be sustained.

passages.case_title: KAILASHBEN MAHENDRABHAI PATEL & ORS. versus STATE OF MAHARASHTRA & ANR.
passages.passage_text:
Held: Impugned judgment set aside – Criminal proceedings 
were filed with mala fide intention only to harass the appellants – 
Though all the allegations related to demand of dowry, the 
complainant chose not to involve her husband in the criminal 
proceedings – Complainant and her husband distributed amongst 
themselves, the institution of civil and criminal proceedings 
against the appellants with the husband instituting the civil suit and 
the complainant filing criminal proceedings – The provocation for 
the Complaint/FIR was essentially the property dispute between 
father and son and it intended only to further their interest of 
the civil dispute

passages.case_title: VIDYASAGAR PRASAD versus UCO BANK & ANR.
passages.passage_text:
It was contended by the Appellant that there is no 
unequivocal, unambiguous and specific acknowledgement of debt 
owed to Respondent – Financial Creditor in the balance sheet 
entries of Corporate Debtor for the years 2017 and 2019 – The 
CIRP was admitted by the NCLT on the ground that there is

query: Does the ruling in Rai Saheb v. State of Haryana establish that non-examination of independent public witnesses is never fatal when interested family witnesses depose?
rationale: Court distinguished the general rule from Rai Saheb, holding that where interested witnesses have unnatural presence and public witnesses were readily available, rule of prudence requires independent corroboration.

passages.case_title: VIJAY SINGH @ VIJAY KR. SHARMA versus THE STATE OF BIHAR
passages.passage_text:
Ordinarily, there is no rule of law to discard the testimonies 
of the witnesses merely because they were known to the victim 
or belonged to her family. For, an offence may be committed in 
circumstances that only the family members are present at the place 
of occurrence in natural course. However, the present case does 
not fall in such category. In the facts of the present case, the natural 
presence of the eye witnesses at the place of occurrence is under 
serious doubt, as discussed above, and for unexplained reasons, the 
naturally present public persons were not examined as witnesses in 
the matter. The non-examination of natural witnesses such as Doman 
Tenti, Daso Mistry, Soordas, Kumud Ranjan Singh and many other 
neighbours who admittedly came out of their houses to witness the 
offence, coupled with the fact that the projected eye witnesses failed 
to explain their presence at the place of occurrence, renders the 
entire version of the prosecution as improbable and unreliable. The 
eye witnesses, being family members, were apparently approached 
by PW18 who in-formed them about the incident and later, their 
versions were fabricated to make the case credible. Notably, when 
the version put forth by the interested witnesses comes under a 
shadow of doubt, the rule of prudence demands that the independent 
public witnesses must be examined and corroborating material must 
be gathered.

passages.case_title: NIPUN ANEJA AND OTHERS versus STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH
passages.passage_text:
Held: The test that the Court should adopt in this type of cases is 
to make an endeavour to ascertain on the basis of the materials on 
record whether there is anything to indicate even prima facie that 
the accused intended the consequences of the act, i.e., suicide – 
Over a period of time, the trend of the courts is that such intention 
can be read into or gathered only after a full-fledged trial – In the

03.11.2006, did the appellants create a situation of unbearable 
harassment or torture, leading the deceased to see suicide as the 
only escape

query: Under Section 106 of the Evidence Act, does the failure of an accused to explain what happened after being last seen alive with the deceased independently suffice to convict him of murder in the absence of other circumstantial evidence?
rationale: Complex burden of proof doctrine: Section 106 provides an additional link once foundational facts are established, but does not independently establish guilt; whether evidence strictly 'answers' this nuanced question is legally contestable and flagged for human review.

passages.case_title: SAMBHUBHAI RAISANGBHAI PADHIYAR versus STATE OF GUJARAT
passages.passage_text:
Held: Time lag between the accused being last seen with the 
deceased and the sighting of the dead body lying was extremely 
short and accused was to offer a plausible explanation as to how 
he parted company with the deceased and the explanation offered 
must be satisfactory, which he failed to do so, that itself provides 
an additional link in the chain of circumstances
